preamble: Insertion of the alveolar nasal [n] where the older form of a word has none. English inserted an intrusive n before the /dʒ/ of several French-derived agent nouns in -ager and -geour: Middle English scavager and herbergeour became scavenger and harbinger, and Old French passagier gave passenger. Messenger has the same n, already present in its Middle English forms. For the whole group (passenger, harbinger, scavenger, porringer) Wiktionary allows either the plain addition of n or contamination from other suffixes such as Middle English -ing. Before /ɡ/ the intrusive nasal is velar, as in nightingale (Middle English nightegale, 'alteration (with intrusive n)').

examples.from: Middle English scavager (< Anglo-Norman scawageour 'inspector, tax collector')
examples.note: Wiktionary compares messenger and passenger, which gained the same n before /dʒ/; passenger is from Old French passagier 'with intrusive n'.

examples.from: Middle English herberjour, herbergeour (< Old French herbergeor) 'a person sent in advance to arrange lodgings'
